 Vs

case_source: From the Judgment and decree dated 21st August 1982 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka, in S.A. No. 368 of 1974.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J:- I have gone through the judgments written by Badrul Haider Chowdhury and Shahabuddin Ahmaed, JJ. I concur with the judgment of Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.

Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court Division, Dhaka Bench, in Second Appeal No. 368 of 1974.

Respondents filed Title Suit No. 163 of 1968 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, against the defendants praying for partition of the suit lands on declaration of the plaintiffs title in certain share of the suit lands.

2. Plaintiffs case, in short, may be stated that Jobeda Khatun and Md. Hedayet Baksha took raiyati settlement of the suit property of 20 pakhis of land on 2.6.1920 from one Md. Yunus Bepari. It is stated that Jobeda Khatun took settlement of 13 ½  pakhis and Hedayet Baksha took settlement of 6 ½  pakhis of land. While in ejmali possession Hedayet died in 1934 or 1935 leaving behind plaintiffs 1 and 2 and his widow plaintiff No. 3 and the predecessor of defendants 8 to 14 and 15 to 19.

3. Plaintiffs case is that after the death of Hedayet his daughter and widow left the property to the care of Jobeda who possessed the property for and on behalf of the co-sharer and the plaintiffs are thus in constructive possession of the suit land. The ejmali character or the suit land has been causing inconvenience, hence the suit for partition with a prayer for declaration of the plaintiffs title.

4. Defendants 1 to 7 contested the suit by filing a written statement. They claimed through late Alfazuddin Ahmed who purchased the property from Jobeda Khatun in 1939, Their case was that Jobeda alone possessed the entire suit land exclusively and adversely in open assertion over the title thereto. Hedayet never possessed the suit land. Jobeda Khatun earlier mortgaged by way of conditional sale 7 pakhis of laud in 1935 and subsequently sold the said laud to Alfazuddin Ahmed in 1939. Thus Alfazuddin acquired  by purchase the entire suit land. Till his death in 1962 he executed as many as 7 registered kabuliyats during the period of 1936-1961 and after his death his heirs defendants 1 to 7 had been possessing the land on payment of rent exclusively for more than 12 year; in assertion of their hostile title to the knowledge of all including the heirs of Hedayet Baksha.

5. The trial court on consideration of the evidence, dismissed the suit and the finding was that no evidence was led that Hedayet had paid any rent for his share of land nor his name was recorded in the landlord's sherista or in the relevant khatian. The trial court came to the conclusion that whatever interest Hedayet had in the suit property extinguished on account of adverse possession by Jobeda Khatun openly for more than 12 years and as such the heirs of Hedayet i.e, plaintiff and the other defendants 8 to 41 cannot lay any claim over the suit property.

6. The appellate court below, however. decreed the suit after setting aside the Judgment and decree of the trial court and decreed the suit of the plaintiffs for partition, on declaration of the title to the extent of 5 pakhis 2 gondas 2 karas and 2 krants out of the lands shown in the schedule.

Defendants preferred Second Appeal No. 368 of 1974. The learned Single Judge affirmed the order of the appellate court below and dismissed the appeal.

Leave was granted to consider the question whether the suit was hit by law of limitation.

7. It is admitted that Elahi Baksha, husband of Jobeda Khatun, had two brothers, Hedayet Baksha and Rebat Baksha and one sister Jarina. Elahi Baksha died leaving his widow Jobeda and children. Hedayet died in 1934 or 1935 leaving his wife and 2 daughters, who are the plaintiffs. Rehat Baksha survived by his heirs who are defendants 8 to 14 and Jarina left behind her heirs defendants 15 to 19. Defendants 22 to 41 have been impleaded since they are the owners of the rest of the land and they have been made parties as the suit was one for partition. Elahi Baksha lived at the residence of his father-in-law at Kaliganj where he died in 1320 B.S. leaving his wife Jobeda Khatun and children. It seems after the death of Elahi Baksha his brother Hedayet Baksha lived in the house of Jobeda's father for some time and looked after her affairs. The land in C. S. Khatian No. 105 (5.16 acres of land) of mouza Kaliganj originally belonged to one Yunus Bepari, who settled with Jobeda Khatun, wife of late Elahi Baksha 13½ pakhis of lands equivalent to 3.1 acres and with Hedayet Baksha 6½ pakhis of land equivalent to 1.69 acres by accepting from them a joint registered kabuliyat dated 9th jaistha 1327 B.S. corresponding to 2.6.1920. Since that settlement both the tenants possessed In ejmali the entire 20 pakis of land which is the suit land .

8. As noticed earlier Hedayat Baksha died in 1934 or 1935 leaving behind the plaintiffs, But of 13½  pakis of land Jobeda Khatun gifted 5 pakhis of land in favour of her son Abdul Qayum on 5.9.35 and Abdul Qayum in his turn mortgaged this land to Alfazuddin Ahmed on 22.10.35. Be it noted Rahat Baksha, the other brother of Hedayet Baksha and Elahi Baksha married Alfazuddin's sister. The heirs of Alfazuddin are the appellants, Then on 12.4.39 Jobeda sold the remaining 15 pakhis of land to Alfazuddln Ahmed by Exts. E. and E(1). Thus the whole property was purchased by Alfazuddin Ahmed.

9. Alfazuddin Ahmed died on 12.11.62 The suit was filed in 1968. As noticed that the heirs of Hedayet Baksha are now the plaintiffs and the heirs of Alfazuddin Ahmed are the defendants. The trial court came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case and the suit was hopelessly time barred, and as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any decree. Further Hedayat and his heirs were never recognised as tenants by the landlords and as such Hedayet Baksha or his heirs never acquired any interest in the suit property.

10. The appellate court, on the other band, came to the conclusion that the right, title and interest by Hedayet Baksha in 6½  pakhis of land out of tile suit land had been subsisting and they had not been extinguished in any manner and consequently the plaintiffs inherited their legal share from Hedayet and they are entitled to get the same. The appellate court below further found that the defence has totally failed to prove that they ever set up a hostile title against the plaintiffs or their predecessor to their knowledge more than 12 years before the institution of this suit. Evidence of P.Ws. 1,3 and 4 was considered, which showed that the plaintiff’s had knowledge of the sale of the suit land by Jobeda Khatun although there was no evidence when the plaintiffs derived the knowledge of the same. Knowledge of Rehat Baksha, who was the husband of the sister of Alfazuddin as attesting witness of Exts. E. and E(1) could not be the knowledge of the plaintiff. Considering this relationship the appellate court below observed "there is no doubt that he was very much well affected to Alfazuddin Ahmed," Alfazuddin Ahmed immediately after his purchase created temporary lease by as many as 7 kabuliyats exts. B series through different persons in respect of the suit laud from 1936 to 1961. The appellate court below commented that by successive transfer by Exts. B series he thought, wrongly though "that he would thereby be in a position to extinguish, the title of Hedayet and his heirs." The appellate court below carefully considered the evidence and came to the conclusion that the right, title and interest of Hedayet Baksha had subsisted and his heirs are entitled to demand partition. Accordingly, the suit was decreed.

11. The High Court Division concurred with the finding that Hedayet Baksha was in joint possession with Jobeda Khatnn, It was observed:

"The exclusive possession of Jobeda Khatun as alleged has not been proved and there is no finding by the court of fact in that behalf to attract the question of limitation to the instant suit."

The High Court Division repelled the contention of adverse possession and considered the possession of a co-owner becomes adverse to other co-owners from the moment when there is an outer or exclusion, that is, an assertion of a hostile title by one co-owner as against the others and that to the knowledge of the latter. It was noticed that these elements bad not been proved by the defendants. Sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession, Reliance was placed on long line of decisions specially in the case of Bindu Bala De Vs. Rebati Mohan De reported in 4 DLR 293. In this view of the matter. the order and judgment of the appellate court below was affirmed and the suit was decreed.

12. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants argued since 1939 Alfazuddin is in possession after his purchase Vide Exts. F and F (1) and therefore, his possession will be adverse to the plaintiffs. Mr. Pal argued that the defendants were in possession openly and to the knowledge of the plaintiff and such overt act is enough to constitute as ouster. Reliance was placed on some highest authorities claiming title by adverse possession 46 I.A. 46 and 61 LA. 78. Mr. Pal further argued that conception or Hindu caste cannot be imported in the facts of this case nor of law of agency can be applied, inasmuch as, no relevant evidence was given on that point. The question of equity does not come, it is contended, since it is the law that should be applied. Mr. Pal argued heavily on two decisions 23 Bom 137 and AIR 1942 Mad (F.B.) 622.

13. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, argued that the kabuliyat was in the joint name of Jobeda Khatun and Hedayet. In the petty settlement of 1933 only 13½  pakhis of land was recorded in the name of Jobeda. Hedayet died in 1934 in 1935. Thereafter Jobeda Khatun gifted 5 pakhis to Qayum, her son, and on 20.10.35 Jobeda mortgaged 15 pakhis of land to Alfazuddein on 22.10.35. Qayum mortgaged his 5 pakhis to Alfazuddin. Thus Alfazuddin was in possession of entire 20 pakhis.

14. Now the second phase: on 10.8.38 Qayum sold his mortgaged land to Alfazuddin and on 12.4.39 Jobeda Khatun sold her mortgaged land to Alfazuddin. Now third phase: from 1939 to 1962 it seems that the parties were not at loggerheads. It was only in 1968 that the suit was filed. Mr. Ahmed argued that there is no trouble so far as the defendants are concerned because it is the matter between the relations and the suit land is situated at a distance of one mile of the plaintiffs' residence. Evidence was given that the plaintiffs got usufruct from the defendents, Finding of fact of the appellate court below and the High Court Division are that Hedayet had a title. Till Hedayet's death no case of adverse possession was made out and after Alfazuddin's purchase he became a co-sharer. Therefore, the question of adverse possession does not arise. Mr. Ahmed contended that the criticism tint plaintiffs obtained usufruct from time to time is not based on the pleading does not merit consideration, in as much as, positive evidence had been given by the plaintiffs that they not only had cordial relationship with Jobeda Khatun and Atfazuddin, but they were given also the usufruct from time to time. Evidence is there even in 1965 that usufruct was demanded from Jobeda. In this view of the evidence it is contended that the defendants had failed to make out achy case of adverse possession.

15. The plaintiff’s case was that the suit lands are ejmali and a co-sharer’s possession of ejmali property is the possession of all co-sharers. Since it has become inconvenient to possess the land in ejmali they brought the suit for partition. The defendants case was that Jobeda had been possessing the entire 20 pakhis of land in her exclusive raiyati rights on payment of rent in her name for the entire and on open assertion of hostile right and title against others. Hedayet, brother of Elahi Baksha staking advantage of illiteracy of the pardanashyn Jobeda Khatun fraudulently managed to create the kabuliyat in question and put forth a claim over the suit property in an attempt to make illegal gains" and Alfazuddin purchased the entire 20 pakhis for good consideration and since his purchase possessed the same "openly and publicly adversely to all subject to the right of Jobeda Knatun and Abdul Qayum for repurchase." In the additional written statement a further stand was taken that though Jobeda drove out Hedayet on detection of the fraud "who appeared to have fraudulently joined in a kabuliyat taking advantage of his position and no heir of Hedayet ever possessed any part of the suit land aid they had no right title or interest in the suit property.

16. Evidence was led by both the sides P.W. 1. is the husband of Plaintiff No. 1, Plaintiff No. 2 is his sister-in-law and No. 3 is his mother-in-law, P.W. 1 stated that Alfazuddin as his distant cousin. These plaintiffs demanded their land from Jobeda who said that the sold away her lands to Alfazuddin. On their demand Alfauddin  told them that he would give crops to plaintiffs where upon plaintiff-3 agreed to the settlement.  Alfazuddin used to possess through borgadars. P.W. 3 Rahima wife of Hedayet stated that Alfazuddin used to deliver crop to the extent of 1/3rd share till he teas alive. In cross-examination she conceded that she had no witness to prove delivery of crop by Jobeda or Alfazuddin. She stated that they did not pay rent to the suit land. P.W. 4 Firoza, daughter of Hedayet  stated that Alfazuddin used to deliver crop. In cross she reiterated that Alfzauddin used to deliver crop to her  mother.

17. D.W. 1 denied the suggestion  that his father Alfazuddin used to deliver crop to the wife of Hedayet. D.W. 2 stated Jobeda alone paid rent to his father Yunus Bepari and denied the suggestion that they granted rent receipts to Jobeda and Hedayet jointly. Analysts of the, evidence do not make out a case of complete ouster so as to justify tine claim of adverse possession. As noticed the parties are inter related and Alfazuddin's sister was married by Rabat, brother of Hedayet and Elahi Baksha.

<u>18. The High Court Division rightly took the view that possession of a co-owner became adverse to others co-owners from the moment from when there is an ouster or exclusion. Reliance was placed in the case of Maharaja Bhupendra Ch. Singha Sarma & ors. Vs. Sudhindra Ch. Singha & ors reported in 5 D.L.R. 251. The appellate court below also worded a finding that there was nothing to suggest ouster or exclusion of the plaintiffs from possession. Sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession. The appellate court below took the view that Hedayet possessed the suit land jointly with Jobeda. These findings of the courts below are founded on the evidence and taking into consideration of the facts and circumstances the question emerged whether the possession of the defendants were so hostile and adverse openly so as to justify the claim of adverse possession. Even if there are apparent show of adverse possession whether those circumstances were sufficient to defeat the title of the real owner only because some lack of vigilance can be attributed to the plaintiffs and would in such circumstances relieve the defendant from discharging their onus in support of their claim of adverse possession The onus is very heavy. It is for the defendant to discharge this so as to build up a claim of adverse possession. A thin veneer of adverse possession or semblance of it viewed from the distance would not be sufficient for the defendants to succeed without discharging their heavy onus. They have to do more that their possession was so open and hostile to the knowledge of all that the plaintiffs must have known the notorious fact that the plea of adverse possession is being raised up. When the relationships are such that the co-sharers are led to believe in certain circumstances which are not uncommon as fact of We will those circumstances be taken as evidence of knowledge of adverse possession. Long line of decisions show that is not the case. Plaintiffs' evidence that they got share of their crop from Alfazuddin and prior to that from Jobeda cannot be disbelieved when viewed in the light of relationship. Mere non-payment of rents and even non-sharing of profit would got justify a case of adverse possession.</u>

<u>19. It is not necessary to recapitulate the principle that has been laid down on the law  of adverse possession by the highest authority. In Secretary of State for India V. Devendra Lal Khan reported in 61 I A. 78=38 C.W. N. 285, the Privy Council laid down what constitutes adverse possession and observed:</u>

<u>As to what constitutes adverse possession, a subject which formed the topic of some discussion in the case, their Lord-ships adopt the language of Lord Robertson in delivering the judgment of the Board in Radhamoni Devi Vs Collector of Khulna " (27 I.A. 136), wisest his Lordship said that 'the possession required must be adequate in continuity in publicity and In extent to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor…………………………</u>

<u>It is sufficient that the possession should be overt and without any attempt at concealment, so that the person against whom rime is running ought, if he exercises due vigilance, to be aware of what is happening:"</u>

<u>20. This principle was, however, not only re-affirmed in Maharaja Srischandra Nandy and ors v. Bajjnath Jugal Kishore (affirm) reported in 39 C.W.N. 352 and it was explained further that when the party claiming by adverse possession fails to show that the patty possessed against, by exercising due vigilance, ought to have been aware of what was happening, his claim must fail, whether his possession be adequate in continuity and extent or not. Their Lordships considered that the real question in cases of this type is whether there were things to be seen which the patty possessed against, being reasonably vigilant, ought to have seen, and, so seeing would have been put on his guard. Consequently, even if there were signs of adverse possession which were sufficient, when seen to put the real owner on his guard, if the signs were such that failure to notice them cannot be said to have involved lack of reasonable vigilance, the onus lying on the adverse claimant is not discharged and his claim of adverse possession must fail.</u>

<u>21. Facts and circumstances of this case attract the application of this principle as laid down in 39 C.W.N. 352 (P.C). Here the parties are interrelated and the distance between the land in question and the home of Hedayet is only one mile. Evidence was led that Jobeda and thereafter Alfazuddin used to deliver craps to the plaintiffs as their share. It may be that this was not done regularly and the criticism of Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed that at the longest it could be said that defendants were dodging the plaintiffs and led them to believe that the ejmali property was still in co-sharership because Alfazuddin being a relation could not be taken as a stranger and as such Alfazuddin's possession could not be a possession for supporting a claim of adverse possession. Nothing, emerged from the facts of the case which ought to have put the plaintiffs on their guard; nothing suspicious was found so as to prove the plaintiffs suspicion about the real motive of Alfazuddin. No signs were apparent to put the plaintiffs on the notice of adverse possession. In these circumstances there is no hesitation in saying that the defendants failed to discharge their onus of establishing a claim by adverse possession. In this view of the matter, the High Court Division was correct in taking the view that there was no ouster of Hedayet Baksha or the plaintiffs nor is there any case of limitation.</u>

In the result, therefore, this appeal is dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.--I have gene through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother, B.H. Chowdhury-J, but I regret my inability to agree with him. I would therefore give my own judgment as follows: This is defendants' appeal. The principal question therein is whether the High Court Division is well founded in law and fact in rejecting their contention that the plaintiff's suit for title and partition is barred by limitation under Article 144 of the Limitation Act in view of their alleged adverse possession of over 30 years as Stranger-Purchaser of the whole of the joint property.

23. The suit land measuring 20 pakhis, equivalent to 5.21 acres, originally belonged to one Younus Bepari. Plaintiffs' (respondents) case is that this laud was settled in raiyati right to Jobeda Khatun and Hedayet Baksh under a registered kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920; share of Jobeda Khatun was 14½  pakhis and that of Hedayet Baksh was 6½  pakhis. Both Jobeda and Hedayet Baksh possessed the land jointly. Hedayet, who lived in Jobeda's house in village Kaliganj left this village and settled in village Zinjira a few miles away but he continued to possess the land jointly with Jobeda till he died sometime in 1933-1934 AD. On his death his widow and two daughters (who are the plaintiffs)along with his brother Rabat Baksh and sister Jarina inherited his 6½  pakhis and since then they had been in constructive possession of the land through Jabeda.  Jabeda transferred five pakhis of land front her share to her son Abdul Qaayum by a registered Deed of Gift dated 5 September 1934. Thereafter, both Jobeda and her sea Quaiyum mortgaged their respective shares to Alfazuddin, predecessor-in-interest of defendants-appellants Nos. 1 to 7 by two separate Deeds of Mortgage dated 22 October 1935. The mortgage was followed by sale to the mortgagee under two registered Sale-deeds one dated 10 August 1938 and the other dated 12 April 1939. Since then Alfazuddin possessed the joint property as a co-sharer of the plaintiffs. Now inconvenience of joint possession being felt the plaintiffs filed the suit for simple partition to the extent of 5 pakhis 2 gondas. On objection hazing been raised the plaint was amended and a prayer far establishment of title was included in the plaint.

24. The suit was resisted by the defendants, who are heirs of Alfazuddin, by a written statement. They totally denied any title of Hedayet Baksh from the very beginning of the kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920. Their case is that the settlement under the kabuliyat was taken by Jobeda alone with her own money and for her own benefit and interest, but Hedayet Baksh who was brother of Jobeda's husband and was brought to her house to look after her affairs on her husband's death, fraudulently got his name inserted in the kabuliyat. That is why Hedayet was not recognized as a tenant by the landlord nor his name was mutated in the landlord's Sherista nor did he possess the land nor paid any rent but jobeda alone possessed the entire land and paid rent first to the landlord and then to the Government after State Acquisition. By the two Mortgage-deeds (as referred to above) Jobeda and her son Quaiyum, had first mortgaged the entire suit land to Alfazuddin and thereafter sold the entire land to him by two registered Sale-deeds whereupon Alfazudditn who was a stranger, entered into possession as owner and possessed it all through openly in assertion of his own title to the exclusion of the plaintiffs and others including Hedayet's brother Rahat and sister Jarina; from the date of settlement in 1920 till the filing of the suit in 1968 no claim of partition or for any usufruct of the land was made by Hedayet and after his death by his heirs, the plaintiffs; the suit was filed malafide as a test case for grabbing the property; the suit was barred by limitation.

24A. Plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses but adduced no documentary evidence except the admitted kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920 (Ext 1). Defendants examined 4 witnesses and produced a number of documents including seven registered Barga-kabutiyats, 18 Rent receipts and some khatians besides the undisputed Mortgage Deeds and Sale Deeds in favour of Alfazuddin. On consideration of these materials the trial Court found that except Hedayet's name appearing in the kabuliyat, Ext 1, there is no evidence whatever that he took settlement of the land along with Jobeda, that Hedayet was neither recognized as a tenant by the landlord nor did he pay any rent nor did he participate in any usufruct of the land and that it is Jobeda who alone possessed the land allthrough till she and her son transferred the entire suit land first by mortgage and then by out-right sale to Alfazuddin. The trial Court further found that Alfazuddin possessed the entire land to the exclusion of the plaintiffs claiming title for himself and that even if Hedayet had originally got any title to the extent of 6 ½   pakhis under the kabuliyat. Ext. 1, his title was extinguished by adverse possession of Jobeda and her transferee. On appeal, the learned District Jude reversed these findings and held that Hedayet had got his title to the extent of 6 ½  pakhis under the kabuliyat and possessed the land jointly with Jobeda and after transfer of the land to Alfazuddin, me plaintiff's possessed the land through Alfazuddin who was their co-sharer whose possession was not adverse to the plaintiffs. This finding bas been concurred in by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division against whose decision this appeal has been preferred as already stated in the judgment of my learned brother B.H. Chowdhury. J.

25. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Advocate for the defendants- appellants, has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Single Judge rejecting the appellants contention of adverse possession from the beginning of the settlement, more particularly from 1935 when Jobeda and her son mortgaged the entire land to Alfazuddin, a stranger. The learned Counsel does not dispute the general principle of law that possession of a co-sharer in a joint property is possession on behalf of other co-sharers as well and that joint possession Continues till other co-sharers are completely ousted by exclusive possession in assertion or hostile title, publicly and openly for a period of 12 years; but he contends that the position is quite different in the instant case where a stranger entered into possession on the claim of exclusive title for the whole of the property. The possession of such a stranger transferee, the learned counsel contends, is adverse light from the beginning who in fact is not a co-sharer. As to knowledge of the co-owners about adverse possession, the learned Counsel contends that it is not necessary that the person claiming adverse possession on claim of hostile title should bring the matter to the knowledge of his transferor's co-sharers but it is sufficient that he possessed the land openly without any attempt to conceal it from the co-sharers and that he possessed it on claim of his exclusive title, The learned Counsel further contends that even if the stranger purchaser's title was defective or invalid still it does not matter so far as his possession is concerned and that the adverse possession begins right from his entry into possession. In the instant case the learned Counsel contends, the plaintiffs were fully aware of the defendants  possession on claim of title of the whole of the suit land.

26. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents, has stoutly defended the High Court Division's decision and contended that Alfazuddin by entering into possession of the suit land became a co-sharer with the plaintiffs no matter his sale-deeds evidenced transfer to him of the entire ejmali land; the sale-deeds are invalid to the extent of the plaintiff's share and as such they continued to be co-sharers in the joint property and that joint-possession shall be presumed to continue till the defendants prove complete ouster of the plaintiffs by adverse possession for 12 years. The learned Counsel has pointed out that plaintiffs predecessor Hedayet, had acquired title in the suit land to the extent of 6½  pakhis ad that this title could not have been extinguished except upon complete ouster on claim of hostile title a case which was not established by the defendants in this suit.

27. As it appears clearly, a. review of the evidence is necessary to determine the real question involved in this appeal, particularly when it centres found loss of title by adverse possession which is itself mixed question of law and fact. The first  point is whether Hedayet had acquired any title by kabuliyat Ext. 1 dated 2-6-1920 A.D. on the face of it he did acquire 6 ½  pakhis along with Jobeda Khatun Whose share was 13 ½  pakhis; whereas defendants totally denied such title, Widow of Hedayet (P.W.3) is one of the plaintiff. In her deposition she claimed that her husband had paid salami and acquired his interest under the kabuliyat but regarding the sources of salami or whether her husband got any means to procure this money she did not say anything. On the other hand, evidence adduced by both D.W. 1. son of Alfazuddin and P.W.1, son-in-law of P.W.3 read along with pleadings of both the parties, clearly shows that Hedayet (brother of Jobeda's husband) bad neither any land nor any house of his own that whatever ancestral landed property he had lie sold it away and resided in the house of Jobeda and after his exit. from that house he lived in the house of his father-in-law in a different village, Zinjira, a few miles away from Jobeda's village in which the suit-bud was situated. Jobeda on the other hand got sufficient resources both from her father and her late previous husband and that at her request Hedayet lived in her house from where he was driven out by her. This claim of the defendants in the written statement has not been disputed. Therefore evidence on record does not give any indication about Hedayet's means to pay for the salami, Be that as it may for the sake of argument I would take that he had paid the salami for his share and acquired title to the extent of 6½  pakhis of the property. But us to possession, evidence of P.W.3 is that Hedayet possessed his share jointly with Jobeda. Such possession, even if accepted continued only for a year or two, for he left the village Kaliganj where the land lay and settled in Zinjira from where he could have possessed only through Jobeda, But admitted fact is that his name was not mutated in the landlord's Sherista nor did he pay any rent nor his name was recorded in the Petty Settlement khatian Ext D (1) which was published some time in 1933. Ext. D(1) recorded Jobeda's name as owner in-possession to the extent of 13 ½  Pakhis in one of the two khatians, The trial Court held that non-participation in any profits from the land, non-payment of any rent and non-recording of his name either in tile landlord's sherista or In any record-of-rights showed that he got no title in the land tinder the kabuliyat which was not acted upon in his case. But the appellate Court took the view that since Hedayet was a co-sharer under the kabuliyat non-participation in profits or non-payment of rent would not extinguish his title. This is true, hut if Jobeda's title was hostile from the very beginning, then by her adverse possession Hedayet's title had extinguished by the time he died, I shall, however not take this view as Hedayet's name appeared in the kabuliyat and presume that he was  a co-sharer of Jobeda with or through whom he possessed his share and that the joint possession continued even after his death and see the subsequent development.

<u><u>28. There is no dispute that Jobeda and her son Quaiyum transferred their entire interests first by mortgage in 1935 and then by sale in 1938-39 to AIfazuddin a stranger. Under these documents Alfazuddin entered into possession of the entire land asserting title over it and if this fact was known to Hedayet's heirs, then Alfazuddin's possession became adverse from the date of his entry into possession. The learned District Judge took the view that for adverse possession it must be brought to the notice of co-sharers and that in this case there was no evidence of such knowledge. This observation is not correct for besides these plaintiffs (who are two daughters and the widow), Hedayet left one brother Rabat Baksh and one sister Jarina as his heirs. Rahat Baksh and Jarina never claimed any share in the land as co-sharer of Alfazuddin. On the contrary Rahat Baksh was a witness to the Sale-deeds, Ext. E and E(1), by which Alfazuddin purchased the entire suit, land including his (Rahat) own interest, if any, therein. The learned District Judge observed that Rahat had married Alfazuddin sister and as such he intentionally kept the matter concealed from the plaintiffs acting in collusion with Alfazuddin. This observation is based on mare conjecture. For no where in the plaint or in the evidence the plaintiffs took such a plea that Rahat had married Alfazuddin's sister and acted in collusion with Alfazuddin or that he bad intentionally suppressed the fact of transfer of the land. Rather P.W. 2. Firoza one of the two daughters of Hedayet sated that her uncle Rahat  Baksh "used to maintain us "Rahat was a government servant and understood the implication  of the transfer to the entire suit land to a stranger under Sale-Deeds. His interest in the land  as common with the plaintiffs interest and he had no reason to keep the transfer suppressed. It is D.W. 1, son of Alfazuddin, who asked whether Rahat had married his father's sister and his answer was in the affirmative. But even if Rabat had married Alfazuddin's sister, there is no evidence that the marriage took place before this transaction, for if he had married after he attested the Transfer Deed then he had no reason to suppress it. In the absence of any plea taken by the plaintiffs, the learned District Judge went off the track to make out a case as to suppression of fact by Rahat.</u></u>

<u><u>29. As to possession since Hedayet's death in 1933 till the filling of the suit in December 1968 P.Ws 1, 3 and 4 (plaintiffs 1, 2 end 3) stated before the Court that Jobeda and after the sale, Alfazuddin used to give them usufructs of the laud occasionally, P.Ws. 1 and 4, however, admitted that they had no personal knowledge about the usufructs but P.W. 3 claimed such personal knowledge of delivery of usufructs. Her statement can hardly be relied upon since it is for the first time in court that this story has been given. It was not mentioned in the plaint; a vital matter like this which is the only link between the plaintiffs and the land For such a long period could not have been missed from the plaint. This claim is contradicted by the paint itself in which a different claim was made regarding possession. There it was stated that after Hedayet’s death the lend was left to the care of Jobeda and through her the plaintiffs maintained  constructive  possession, "Constructive possession" is not actual possession  it is possession of one on behalf of another such as, possession of a co-sharer who possesses not only for himself  but also for other co-sharers who need not participate in any profit or benefit from the land  in that case the actual possession of one person is deemed to be possession of other co-sharers as well. Enjoyment of usufructs means actual possession. Paragraph 5 of the plaint in which they claim constructive possession is quoted below :</u></u>

<u><u>“5. That on the death of Hedayet Box, his heirs daughters and widow left the property to the care of Jobeda Khatun and she possessed on behalf of the other co-sharers of the property and the plaintiffs are in constructive possession of tire suit land ; moreover one co-sharer's possession of ejmali property is the possession of all the co-sharers."</u></u>

<u><u>30. In is therefore clear that the story of collecting usufruct is a new one introduced for the first time in court in a feeble attempt to maintain a link with the land, a link which had otherwise been snapped long ago. The First Appellate Court's finding that the plaintiffs possessed their share by enjoying usufructs is based on a matter disclosed for the first time in evidence in court. This finding is not worth considering, as has been observed in clear language by the Privy Council in the case of Siddik Mohammad Sha vs Nt. Faran, AIR 1930 PC 57 as quoted below:</u></u>

<u><u>"Where  a claim has been never made in the defence presented no amount of evidence can be looked into upon a plea which was never put forward before."</u></u>

31. P. W. 3, Hedayets widow, admitted that her husband did not Pay any rent for the land. Defendants claimed to have paid rent all-through and produced 18 Receipts, Ext. 'C' series; first 10 Receipts were purportedly granted by the ex-landlord to Jobeda and then to Alfazuddin alone, and the next 8 Receipts were granted to Alfazuddin by the Government Estate Office. The learned District Judge. however, went to the extent of disbelieving these receipts taking the ground that in three Receipts payment of rent by Jobeda was recorded in the landlord's portion of the Receipts and that the counterfoils were not produced, etc. The defect of recording the payment in the wrong part of the Receipts might have been due to carelessness of the receiving clerk and this mistake relates to only three Receipts; but in the remaining 15 Receipts including those from the Government Tahsil office there is no defect. Rejection of all these Receipts "as false and fabricated" is unwarranted and finding on this point is clearly perverse and this erroneous finding is found to have materially affected the District Judge's decision on the question or possession.

32. Another piece of evidence of defendants possession is seven registered Barga Kabuliyats, Ext. B series. Evidence of D.W. 1. which is supported by P.W. 4, is that his father possessed the land though different bargaders. He produced these Barga Kabuliyats Executed by the respective Borgaders over a period of 25 years, the first one being dated 2-6-36 and the last one being dated 4-4-02. These bargaders delivered adhi-share not to the plaintiffs but to Alfazuddin alone. We find no basis for the observation of the learned District Judge that these Barga Kabuliyats might have been created for the purpose or fabricating evidence of title.

<u>33. From the evidence discussed above, I find two distinct stages of possession of the laud, first one from 1920 to 1934 that is, from the date of Kabuliyat Ext. 1 till the death of Hedayet, and the second one from the time of Hedayet's death till the filing of the suit in 1968, more particularly from transfer of the land to Alfazuddin in 1935. For the sake of argument I would accept that Hedayet was a co-sharer under Ext. 1 in 1920 and also that he was in constructive possession of his share through Jobeda and then see whether the law of adverse possession came in operation against his heirs from 1935 when Alfazuddin, a stranger, on claim of 16-annas title, began to possess the  land alone. A co-sharer's possession is possession on behalf of all co-sharers and this possession is presumed to continue till other co-sharers are ousted completely by exclusive possession openly on claim of hostile title by another co-sharer. This principle of law was propounded by the Judicial Committee of tile Privy Council in the case of Corea Vs. Apuhamy AIR 1914 PC 243, in which Lord Macnaughten cited the dictum of V.C. Wood In Thomas vs. Thomas that possession is never considered adverse if it is referred to a lawful title. Similar view had been expressed  much earlier by Lord ,Denman C.J. in Culley  v. Doe Dem Taylerson. 11A & E. 1008 (1840) in the following terms:</u>

<u>"Generally speaking one tenant is common cannot maintain an ejectment against another tenant in common, because the possession of the tenant in common is the possession of the other, and to enable the party complaining to maintain an ejectment, there must be an ouster of the party complaining. But where the claimant, tenant in common, has not teen in the participation of the rents and profits for a considerable length of time and other circumstances concur, the Judge will direct the jury to take into consideration whether they will presume that there has been an Ouster."</u>

<u>Mr. Khondaar Mahbubuddin Ahmed argued that in spite of Alfazuddin's Mortgage-Deeds and Sale-Deeds showing transfer of the whole of the land to him, plaintiffs share remained unaffected and they continued as co-sharers of Alfazuddin and as such it is only their complete ouster, the onus of which lies on the defendants, that their title could be lost by adverse possession.</u>

34. Mr. S.R. Pal is not ready to accept Alfazuddin as a co-sharer of the plaintiffs at all in view of the fact that the whole of the property was transferred to a stranger who entered into the land as a trespasser; his possession was adverse right from the beginning.

<u>35. In support of their respective contentions the learned counsels cited a great number of decision. In Bhavrdo  v. Rakhmin,  23 Bom 137 (F.B.), some co-parceners of a joint family estate alienated  by mortgage and safe "certain defined and distinct portions" of the joint estate to a stranger who began possession claiming exclusive title. In a suit for partition by other co-perceners the plea of adverse possession taken by the alignee  was accepted by the court. In that case Article 127 of the Limitation Act was not held applicable as this Article applies only in cases between the members of a joint family and net to the case of a stranger in whose case Article 144 applies. As to the purchaser's possession it was held :</u>

<u>"The answer, we think, must be than as he enters as owner and in right of his conveyance, his possession is adverse to them also. In the eve of law, all the co-parceners though for the sake of convenience they may be in separate possession of portions of the joint estate, are the owners of the whole estate including the alienaled portion. It may be and indeed is the case that such a purchaser by his purchase does not get a good title to the land conveyed to him by a Sink co-parcener, but only the qualified right laid down in Pardurang v. Bhaskar (supra), and he is liable under some circumstances even to be evicted if the co-parceners take the requisite steps within the statutory period Nevertheless, his exclusive possession does not en that account case to be adverse. He, entering as owner, his possession must, we think, necessarily be adverse to the true owners. Adverse possession depends upon the claim to title under which the possessor holds and not upon a consideration of the question in whom the true ownership is vested whether in a single person or in many jointly."</u>

<u>36. The principle laid done in this ease vies followed in the case of Pillai v. Amjadul, AIR 1942 Mad. 622 ( FB). In that case, possession of a mortgagee in a share of a joint property belonging to a Muslim family was held to be adverse against his mortgagor's co-sharers and the suit by other members of the family for recovery of possession was held barred by limitation under Article 144, Limitation Act. As to knowledge of the adverse possession, it was observed that it was sufficient that possession was overt and without any attempt at concealment so that the person against whom time was running ought, if be exercised due vigilance, to be aware of what was happening. It was observed:</u>

<u>"When one of several co-sharers leis into possession a stranger who proceeds to cultivate the land for his own behalf the other co-sharers must unless they deliberately close their eyes, know of what is going on, but if they are so regardless of their own interests they must take the consequences. Where a person who is in possession under a usufructuary mortgage granted by one of several co-parceners remains in possession of the land and cultivates it for years, a position which we have here, there can be no doubt that the requirements of continuity, publicity and extent for adverse possession are fully complied with."</u>

37. In this connection Mr. Pal has referred to a observation of the Privy Council in the case of Radhamoni Devi V. Collector of khulna, and others 27 I.A. PC 136 to the effect that : "

"To constitute a plaintiff's title by adverse possession, the possession required to be proved must be adequate in continuity, in publicity, and in extent, and is displaced by evidence of partial possession by the defendant,"

Mr. Pal contends that the defendants case fully fits into this principle as laid down and fulfills all the requirements of acquisition of title by adverse possession. In the case before us the principle as to acquisition of title by adverse possession has not been invoked by the plaintiffs, but it has been invoked by the defendants to maintain their possession under mortgage-deeds followed by sale-deeds for over a period of 30 years, a possession which was open without any concealment and in the exercise of hostile title.

<u>38. The next case relied upon by Mr. Pal is Bharat Pillai V. Jeebarahmal, 46 IA, PC 285. There, possession of one co-shares was held to be adverse against the other co-sharer of a joint property. The Judicial Committee took note of the general principle that one tenant in common could not maintain an ejectment suit against another tenant in common in ordinary circumstances bra, the Committee held, where the letter tenant had not been in participation of rent and profits for a condonable length of time and other circumstances concurred then the court should hold ouster 'of the latter tenant. Mr. Pal has tried to reinforce his argument that if a stranger enters upon possession of any ejmali property either in whole or in part under any conveyance executed by one of several co sharers, then though the conveyance is invalid the stranger's possession is adverse right from the beginning and this possession ripens into title on the expiry of the statutory period of 12 years. In Lala Hem Chand V. Lala Peary Lal and others, AIR 1942, PC 64, a defendant claimed title by adverse possession on the basis of a trust which was held to be void on the ground of vagueness as to its contents. The plaintiffs' suit for ejectment was dismissed and it was held:</u>

<u>"Where a trustee has been in possession for upwards of 12 years. of property under a trust which is void under the law, an action against hint by the rightful owner would be barred by imitation under the statute, the reason being that the possession of a trustee is as much adverse to the true owner as that of any trespasser."</u>

<u>39. In the case of Adiluddin Vs. Chandra kumar 5 PLR (Dac), 302, a learned Single Judge held that possession of a stranger  purchaser of the whole of an ejmali property could not be construed as possession of a co-sharer when the stranger entered into possession claiming that be was owner of the entire property by a sale-deed, no matter the sale-deed was void. Facts of the case are that a joint family property belonged to two brothers Bhajan and Prahiadh Bhajan died leaving a widow and a minor son Bhuban; the widow sold the entire share inherited from her husband by her and her son to Prahlad by a sale-deed whereupon Prahlad entered into possession. The defendant purchased from Prahlad the entire ejmali property which previously belonged to him and his late brother by a sale-deed. Bhaban on attaining majority transferred his share to the plaintiffs who then filed a suit for partition invoking the principle, that the sale by his mother was invalid so far as his share was concerned and that Prahlad and after him the defendant possessed the land as his co-sharer and as such that possession was not adverse. This contention was rejected in view of exclusive possession of the defendant right from the beginning of the invalid transfer. Other case referred to by Mr. Pal including "Secretary of State Vs. Debendralal  Khan", 38 MN. PC 285 contain simply reiteration of the same principle that a stranger purchaser of a joint property as a whole, when he enters into possession in exercise of his right and continues in possession in exclusion of other claimants, openly without any attempt at concealment, is not a co-sharer and that his possession is adverse right from the beginning and farther that it is not necessary for him to bring to the notice of the former co-sharers Of his vendor the fact of his adverse possession. As such, I need not refer to all these eases.</u>

<u>40. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, as already state above, does not agree that a stranger purchasing the whole of an ejmali property is not a co-sharer. He contends that such a purchaser, whether he purchases whole of the ejmali property or any share thereof, is also a co-sharer and his possession is governed by the general principle that a co-sharer's possession is possession on behalf of all other co-sharers. He has referred to the case of Muzaffar Khan Vs. Yousuf Khan., PLD (1959) . SC 9. in which the vendee of a co-sharer of an undivided property was held to be a co-sharer and is entitled to pre-emption under the North Western Frontier Province Preemption Act. Balaram Vs. Shyamcharan, 24 CWN 1057, a similar question arose for determination by the Calcutta High Court and it was held that the possession of land, under common title, of one co-owner would not be presumed to be adverse to other co-sharers but ordinarily, it could be held for the benefit of all. It was observed :</u>

<u>"The law will never construe a possession tortious, unless from necessity : on the other hand its gill consider every possession lawful the commencement and continuance of which is not proved to be wrongful and this, upon the principle that every man shall be presumed to act in obedience to his duty, until the contrary appears. In other words, the only difference between the possess slots of a co-owner and other cases is, that acts, which, if done, by a stranger, would perse be a disseisin, are, in the case of tenancies in common,  susceptible of explanation consistently with the real title acts of ownership are not, in tenancies in common, acts of disseisin; it depends upon the intent with winch they are done and their notoriety; the law will not presume that cue tenant in common intends to oust another; the facts must be notorious and the intent must be established in proof."</u>

<u>Facts in this case are that the property belonged to three brothers two of whom had left their ancestral home in the village and settled in another village and were not in possession for 50 years; during this period their brother who stayed back possessed the hind paying rent alone in his name, and dealt with the entire properly as his own and then transferred it to the defendant, a stronger. Plaintiffs purchased 2/3rd share from these two absentee brothers and filed a suit for partition on declaration of title. The defendant pleaded adverse possession as a stranger purchaser, but the contention was rejected on the ground that he became a co-sharer in the land and his possession was on behalf of other two co-sharers and that his possession did not exclude them.</u>

<u>41. The next case relied upon by Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed is Izat Baksh Sarkar v. Abdul Quadir Bhuiyan, 21 DLR (SC) 444. In that case a brother sold certain property to a stranger claiming the property as his own, whereas it belonged to him and his two minor brothers. The purchaser possessed the property openly, exclusively and in assertion of his own title or mutation of his name and by payment of rent. The minors took no step to assert their title for long 21 years even, after they attained majority. In that case the general rule that a co-sharers possession is possession on behalf of other co-sharers was applied and the plea of adverse possession was rejected, The Court, however, observed that this does not mean that a co-sharer can never possess adversely to the other co-sharers and acquire title by adverse possession. To enable one of the co-sharers to acquire title by adverse possession as against the other co-sharers, his possession must be of such an actual, open, notorious, exclusive and hostile character as to amount to an ouster or exclusion of the other co-sharers. Moreover, such possession must be for a continuous period of at least 12 years in assertion of a hostile title to the knowledge of the co-sharers against whom title by adverse possession is claimed. Such knowledge may be proved directly or inferentially," It may be noted that in both these cases original title of the contending co-sharers was not in dispute and that they got the property by inheritance; whereas in the instant case the original title of the plaintiffs predecessor, Hedayet, is in dispute. Kh. Mahbubuddin has also relied upon the following cases where the same principle as to a co sharer's possession has been re-stated and applied. Maroon Mia v. Majiduddin, 4 DLR 114; Bindhu Bala v. Rabati Mohan, 4 DLR 293, Maharaja Bhupendra Singh v. Sudhindra Chandra Singh, 5 DLR 251; Abdul Jalil Shikder  v. Khurshed Ali, 27 DLR AD 143, and & Mohar Ali v. Zafar Ali, 27 DLR 451.</u>

<u>The case of Sabah Lal V. Fated Mohammad, AIR 1932 (All) 393 (FB) has bees relied upon by both Mr, Pal and Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed —the former for the minority view and the latter for the majority view taken therein. In that case the entire joint property, which was a shop was first mortgaged by one of the proprietors to a stranger. The mortgage was followed by sale whereupon the transferee claimed absolute ownership in view of his exclusive possession over 14 years. The claim was resisted by the other proprietor who was no party either to the mortgage or to the sale and he contended that the transferee was his co-sharer when possession was his possession as well. By a majority decision the plaintiff-transferee's claim of adverse possession was rejected, one of the grounds being that if the period or mortgage was excluded and adverse possession was counted from the .date of sale the period of possession fell short of 12 years. The relevant part of the majority decision is quoted below :</u>

<u>"Adverse possession must be within the knowledge of the co-sharer; mere possession by mortgagee from the co-owner does not amount to ouster. A co-owner has no duty cast upon him to watch the conduct of another co-owner and be on lookout to find out the extent of the share purported to be transferred by him and to intervene if more than the real shave has been transferred. He is entitled to assume that the permissive nature of Vie possession has passed on to his co-owner's transferee who has now become the co-owner in place of the original co-owner. Of course if the assertion of title to the whole is brought to his knowledge and it is accompanied by his ouster and exclusion, adverse possession would then commence as against him". The minority view was, however, that "a mortgage of the entire property by one of the proprietors is a clear assertion of adverse title and the possession of the mortgagee is surely adverse to the co-owners of the mortgagors."</u>

<u>42. Now coming back to the instant case, the position of Alfazuddin as I find was that of a trespasser from 1935 if Hedayet had acquired title to the extent of 6 ½  pakhis under the kabuliyat. This was so because Alfazuddin entered into possession of the whole of land on claim of 16-annas title under his title deeds which were invalid to the extent of the plaintiffs share. But whether Alfazuddin entered into possession as a trespasser or as plaintiffs co-sharer, his exclusive possession exercised openly on claim of 16 annas title constituted complete ouster of the plaintiffs; and this possession is certainly adverse and has over the period of 33 years extinguished whatever title the plaintiffs had in the land. This adverse possession was very much within the knowledge of the plaintiffs from the time of this entry into the land. from 1935. This knowledge is clearly established from paragraph 3 of their plaint and also from their total unconcern about the land. As to the knowledge of their co-sharer Rabat Baksh about the transfer, since his interest in the land was common with theirs, there was no season why he would not disclose the matter to them. By the Sale deeds he attested his own interest also was transferred, if he had any. Possession on Alfazadnin was open, in total exclusion of the plaintiffs, on claim of title and without any attempt at concealment over this long period during which plaintiffs had no participation in profits of the land or payment of rent; their names were not recorded in any document nor did they ever claim any benefit from or partition of this land. In fact they had no connection with the land from 1935, and nothing was known about them till they filed the suit, according to the defendants, just to take a chance to establish title. The suit is hopelessly barred under Article 144 of the Limitation Act. Views taken by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division tend to show that once a co-sharer always a co-sharer and that against a co-sharer there can be no extinguishment of title by adverse possession. Plaintiff and before them, their predecessor were completely out of scene from the date of the kabuliyat. In these circumstances, the suit was rightly dismissed by the trial Court.</u>

43. In conclusion, I would set aside the judgment of the High Court Division and restore that of the trial Court. The appeal is allowed without however any order as to costs.

ORDER OF THE COURT

By a majority decision, the appeal is dismissed. There will, however, be no order as to costa.
